titleText: Smart Contract Development Services for Products That Hold Real Value

c.v: Once a smart contract is deployed, it does exactly what its code says. It does this for every user and every attacker, often with no way to stop it. Our smart contract development services are built around that fact. We turn your business rules into on-chain logic, design the permissions and upgrade path before any code is written, and test the system against the ways it can fail. We deliver contracts in a state an independent auditor can review efficiently.
We build on Ethereum and EVM-compatible networks in Solidity and Vyper, on Solana in Rust with Anchor, and on Hyperledger Fabric in Go for permissioned enterprise networks.

title.v: Who Hires a Smart Contract Development Company and Why

c.v: Most projects that reach us fall into one of five situations. Each needs a different kind of engineering attention.
You are launching a token.
You need supply rules, mint and burn authority, vesting for the team and investors, and a distribution plan that holds up to scrutiny from exchanges and holders.
You are building a DeFi protocol.
Pricing, collateral, liquidation and reward logic have to stay correct under adversarial conditions: flash loans, oracle manipulation and MEV.
You are launching an NFT product.
You need mint mechanics that survive a high-demand launch, metadata that will not disappear, and royalty and marketplace logic that matches how the ecosystem actually works.
You are an enterprise team automating a workflow.
You need role-based approvals, a tamper-evident audit trail and integration with the systems you already run, sometimes on a permissioned ledger rather than a public chain.
You already have contracts.
You need an experienced Solidity team to review, extend, upgrade or take over code written by someone else.
For each of these, we start with how the product creates and protects value. Code comes after.

title.v: Before Writing Code: Deciding What Belongs On-Chain

c.v: Not every part of a product belongs in a smart contract. On-chain logic is public, permanent and costs gas to run. Off-chain logic is private, cheap and easy to change. Good smart contract engineering puts each piece of the system in the right place.

title.v: Smart Contract Development Services We Provide

c.v: Custom Smart Contract Development

Custom smart contract development is for products whose rules do not fit a template, such as revenue sharing, conditional escrow, marketplace settlement or a new financial primitive. We write a specification first. It covers the state the contract holds, who can change it, which values must never change, and what happens at every boundary: zero amounts, maximum values, empty pools and duplicated calls. That specification becomes both the test plan and the reference document your auditor reads.
Where a well-reviewed implementation already exists, we build on it rather than reinventing it. In practice this usually means the
OpenZeppelin Contracts
library for tokens, access control, governance and proxies.
Token Smart Contract Development
A token contract is simple to deploy and easy to get wrong commercially. We design and implement:
Standards.
ERC-20 for fungible tokens, with ERC-2612
permit
for gasless approvals where wallets and integrations benefit. SPL tokens on Solana.
Supply logic.
Fixed, capped or controlled-emission supply, with the minting authority defined explicitly and, where appropriate, removed after launch.
Minting and burning.
Who can mint, under what limit, and whether burns are user-initiated, fee-based or programmatic.
Ownership and admin powers.
Every privileged function is documented, held by a multisig rather than a single key, and renounced when it is no longer needed.
Vesting and distribution.
Cliff-plus-linear schedules, revocable or irrevocable grants, and batch distribution. We test edge cases such as revocation in the middle of a cliff and tokens sent to a schedule before it starts.

Holders, exchanges and analysts read token contracts closely. A token with an unexplained mint function or an owner-controlled blocklist creates doubts that no marketing can remove. Our job is to make every power in the contract intentional and visible.
DeFi Smart Contract Development

DeFi contracts hold pooled user funds and are attacked by people who read the code more carefully than most reviewers do. The engineering here is less about writing functions and more about defending the protocol's economics.
Liquidity pools and AMMs.
Invariant-based pricing, fee accounting, slippage and deadline protection, and resistance to price manipulation. Time-weighted prices are used where spot prices can be pushed in a single transaction.
Staking and rewards.
Reward-per-token accounting that stays accurate and costs the same gas whether there are ten stakers or ten thousand. We also handle reward-rate changes and empty-pool states.
Lending and borrowing.
Collateral factors, health-factor calculations, interest-rate models and liquidation incentives. Oracle integrations check that price data is fresh and fall back safely when a feed stalls.
Tokenized vaults.
ERC-4626 vaults with protection against the first-depositor share-inflation attack, and rounding that always favours the vault over the caller.
Protocol economics.
We model what happens at extremes: a 50% price drop in one block, a whale withdrawing all liquidity, rewards running out. Then we encode the expected behaviour as invariants the test suite enforces.
For full protocol builds that include front ends, indexers and tokenomics, see our
DeFi development services
NFT Smart Contract Development
Token standards.
ERC-721 for unique items. ERC-1155 for editions, game items and memberships, where batch transfers save gas.
Minting mechanics.
Allowlists stored as a single Merkle root rather than thousands of on-chain entries. Signature-based mints protected against replay. Per-wallet limits, supply caps and phased sales.
Metadata.

We help you decide between content-addressed storage (IPFS or Arweave) and fully on-chain metadata. We also help you decide when metadata should be frozen so collectors know the artwork cannot be swapped.
Royalties.

We implement ERC-2981 royalty information. We are also clear about its limits: ERC-2981 tells marketplaces what royalty to pay, but marketplaces decide whether to honour it. Where royalties are central to your business model, we discuss enforcement options and their trade-offs.
Marketplace contracts.
Listing, offer and settlement logic, usually with orders signed off-chain and settled on-chain.
For marketplace platforms and full NFT product builds, see our
NFT development services
DAO Governance Contracts

Governance contracts decide who controls the treasury and the protocol's upgrade keys, so a design flaw here can hand over everything at once. We implement token-weighted governance with proposal thresholds, quorum, voting periods and a timelock between a vote passing and its execution. That delay gives token holders time to react to a malicious proposal. We also design the transition from a founding team's multisig to community control, so decentralisation happens in planned stages.
Enterprise Smart Contract Solutions
Enterprise smart contract development has different priorities from consumer Web3: permissions, privacy, data integrity and integration with existing systems.
Role-based access control
that mirrors your organisation, such as maker-checker approvals, department-level permissions and time-delayed administrative actions.
Workflow automation.
Contracts enforce each step of a process, for example a payment that is released only when a delivery is confirmed by the right party, and emit an event at every step for your audit trail.
Data integrity.
Sensitive records stay in your systems. The contract stores hashes and state transitions, which prove a record existed and was not altered without exposing its contents.
Integration.
Event indexing and APIs connect contract activity to your ERP, payment or reporting systems.
Regulated asset tokens.

For tokenized securities and real-world assets, permissioned token standards such as ERC-3643 limit transfers to verified, eligible holders and support the recovery and forced-transfer functions regulators may require. The contract enforces the rules you define; legal structuring and compliance remain a matter for your counsel.
Permissioned ledgers.
Where data must not be public, we build Go chaincode on Hyperledger Fabric, using channels and private data collections to control who sees what.
For broader enterprise programmes, see
enterprise blockchain solutions
. For tokenization platforms, see
asset tokenization platform development
Smart Accounts and Account Abstraction

Wallet friction loses users, and account abstraction can remove much of it. We build ERC-4337 smart accounts and paymaster logic for sponsored gas, session keys and batched actions. We also work with EIP-7702, which has let existing Ethereum wallets delegate to smart-account code since the Pectra upgrade in May 2025. Delegation targets have full control of the account that delegates to them, so we treat them with the same care as a vault contract. If you need the full wallet product as well as the contracts, see
crypto wallet development
Smart Contract Review, Upgrades and Takeover

If your contracts were written by another team or a freelancer who is no longer available, we can take them over. We start with a structured review: architecture, privileged roles, upgrade mechanism, test coverage and known risk patterns. You receive a written report of what we found and what we recommend. We then extend, refactor or upgrade the code under the same testing discipline we apply to new work.
Smart contract languages are not interchangeable. Each one targets a specific execution environment, so the network you choose determines the language, the tooling and the security model.

c.v: Solidity and Vyper Smart Contract Development on EVM Chains
Solidity is the most widely used smart contract language and our primary language for EVM work. Since version 0.8, arithmetic overflow causes a revert by default. We use
unchecked

blocks only where a bound has been proven, for example a loop counter. Custom errors replace revert strings to keep deployment and failure costs down. One Solidity codebase can be deployed across Ethereum and its Layer 2 networks. Each network still needs to be checked for differences in opcode support, block timing and gas pricing before deployment.
We use Vyper where a project's design or an existing codebase calls for it. Its deliberately limited feature set makes some classes of mistakes harder to write.
Rust Smart Contract Development on Solana

Solana programs are written in Rust and work differently from EVM contracts. Programs are stateless, and data lives in separate accounts that must be passed into every instruction. Most Solana security work is therefore about account validation: confirming that every account is owned by the expected program, has the right signer, and is the program-derived address it claims to be. We use Anchor, whose account constraints enforce many of these checks by default, and we review explicitly the cases its constraints do not cover.
Go Chaincode on Hyperledger Fabric

On Fabric, business logic runs as chaincode, which we write in Go. It runs on a network of known organisations, with endorsement policies that specify which participants must approve each transaction. This suits consortium use cases where a public chain's transparency is a drawback rather than a benefit.

title.v: How We Architect a Smart Contract System

c.v: Turning Business Rules into State, Roles and Invariants
Every engagement produces a written specification before implementation starts. It defines:
State.
What the contracts store, for example balances, positions, schedules or listings.
Actors and roles.
Who can call each function: users, operators, guardians, governance.
Invariants.

Statements that must hold after every transaction. For example: "total shares are always backed by vault assets", "no account can withdraw more than it deposited plus earned rewards", or "a vesting schedule can never release more than its grant".
Failure behaviour.
What happens when an oracle is stale, a token transfer fails or a limit is reached.
Invariants are the most valuable part of this document. Every later testing step checks the code against them.
Access Control and Admin Key Design

Most large smart contract losses involve compromised or misused privileged access rather than clever code exploits. Access control is first on the OWASP Smart Contract Top 10 (2026). We design permissions as carefully as business logic:

blocks.alt: Smart contract admin roles held by a multisig and executed through a timelock

c.v: Narrow roles.
A role can pause the contract, set fees or upgrade it, but no single role does all three.
Single-owner contracts.
Ownership transfers in two steps (
Ownable2Step
), so control cannot be sent to a mistyped address.
Multi-contract systems.
Role-based access (
AccessControl
, or OpenZeppelin's
AccessManager
) manages permissions across the system from one place.
Admin keys in a multisig wallet.
Sensitive changes go through a
timelock
, so users can see a pending change before it takes effect.
An admin powers table.
We document every privileged function in a table you can publish for users and auditors.
Upgradeable or Immutable: Choosing Deliberately
Upgradeability lets you fix bugs and add features. It also means users must trust whoever holds the upgrade key, so it should be a deliberate choice rather than a default.

blocks.alt: Upgradeable smart contract proxy architecture separating storage from logic

c.v: Immutable contract

rows.v: Simple tokens, trust-minimised primitives, contracts whose credibility depends on never changing
Thorough pre-launch testing; migration plan if a new version is ever needed

c.v: UUPS proxy

rows.v: Products expected to evolve; upgrade logic kept in the implementation
Upgrade authorisation behind multisig and timelock; checks that each new version keeps the upgrade function

c.v: Transparent proxy

rows.v: Systems where admin and user call paths must be strictly separated
Dedicated proxy admin held by multisig

c.v: Phased approach

rows.v: Early-stage protocols
Upgradeable at launch, with a published plan to lock or hand upgrade rights to governance

c.v: For upgradeable contracts we use namespaced storage layouts (ERC-7201) and automated storage-layout validation. Before every upgrade goes live we rehearse it on a fork of the live network. A storage collision during an upgrade can corrupt every balance in the system, so this step is never skipped.
Gas Optimization Without Sacrificing Clarity

Gas costs are paid by your users on every interaction, so gas optimization improves your product directly. Code that is too clever to audit is a security risk, so we prioritise the optimizations that matter:
Storage design first.

Writing a new storage value is among the most expensive EVM operations. We pack related values into shared storage slots, read storage once per function, and avoid storing data that only off-chain systems need. That data goes into events instead.
Off-chain data with on-chain proofs.
Merkle roots and signatures replace large on-chain lists for allowlists, claims and airdrops.
Compiler-friendly patterns.
constant
and
immutable
for fixed values,
calldata
for read-only inputs, custom errors, and transient storage for locks that only need to last one transaction.
Layer 2 awareness.
On rollups, the cost of publishing transaction data often outweighs execution cost, so we keep inputs compact.
Measured, not guessed.
Gas snapshots are part of the test suite, so any change that makes a function more expensive is visible in review.
Oracles and External Integrations

A contract is only as reliable as the data and contracts it depends on. For price feeds we check freshness and sanity bounds on every read and define what happens when a feed stops updating. For token integrations we handle tokens that do not follow the standard exactly, such as those that charge transfer fees or do not return a success value. For external protocol calls we follow the checks-effects-interactions pattern and apply reentrancy guards where state changes cross contract boundaries.
Security is not a phase at the end of development. It starts with the threat model during architecture and continues through every pull request.
Threat Modeling

Before implementation, we list who might attack the system and how. The list covers external users, other contracts, front-running bots, compromised admin keys, malicious governance proposals and manipulated oracles. Each threat is linked to a mitigation in the design and a test that proves the mitigation works.

c.v: Invariant testing deserves a short explanation. Instead of checking one scenario, the test framework generates long random sequences of deposits, withdrawals, liquidations and transfers, and checks after each step that the system's core properties still hold. It is one of the most effective ways to find bugs that arise only from a specific sequence of actions.
Code coverage is reported for every release.  Coverage shows which code the tests executed, not whether the tests checked the right things. That is why the invariant work above matters.
Vulnerability Classes We Design and Test Against
Access control flaws.
Unprotected functions, overly broad roles, uninitialized proxy implementations.
Business logic errors.
The code does what it says, but what it says is economically exploitable.
Price oracle manipulation.
Spot prices from thin liquidity pools used as trusted inputs.
Flash-loan-funded attacks.
Any logic that assumes a user cannot temporarily control a large amount of capital.
Reentrancy.
Including read-only reentrancy, where another protocol reads inconsistent state mid-transaction.
Unchecked external calls and input validation gaps.
Arithmetic and rounding errors.
Especially in share, interest and reward calculations.
Proxy and upgrade risks.
Storage collisions and unprotected upgrade functions.
Front-running and MEV.
Missing slippage limits and deadlines; predictable values used as randomness.
Signature replay.
Signatures that lack a nonce, chain ID or contract-specific domain.
Denial of service.
Unbounded loops and payouts that one failing recipient can block.

title.v: Development Testing vs. an Independent Smart Contract Audit

c.v: The two are often confused, and the difference matters to your users, investors and exchange partners.

blocks.alt: Comparison of internal smart contract testing and an independent security audit

c.v: What our development process provides:

secure design, a threat model, a complete test suite with fuzz and invariant testing, static analysis and internal peer review of every change. This reduces the number of issues that reach an audit and makes the audit faster and more productive.
What an independent audit provides:
a separate security team with no stake in the code reviews a frozen version of it and publishes its findings. The value is in the independence.
A team should not be the final reviewer of its own code, and our internal review is not presented as an audit.
How we prepare your contracts for audit:
Freeze the scope.
A tagged commit, with the exact files and networks in scope.
Deliver an audit package.
The specification, the admin powers table, the threat model, the invariant list, known limitations and the full test suite.
Coordinate the audit.
We help you select and schedule an independent firm and answer auditor questions during the review.
Remediate.
We fix the findings and return the changes for the auditor's fix review.
Publish.
We help you publish the final report alongside the deployed, verified contract addresses.

No development process or audit can guarantee that a contract is free of vulnerabilities. Testing, independent audits, bug bounties and monitoring each reduce risk in different ways, and production systems holding significant value should use all of them.

Deployment is where small mistakes become expensive: a wrong constructor argument, an admin role left on a deployer's personal key, an implementation contract left uninitialised. We treat deployment as engineering work, not a button press.
Scripted, repeatable deployments.
Every deployment runs from version-controlled scripts, first on a local fork, then on a public testnet, then on mainnet with the same scripts.
Pre-flight checks.
We confirm constructor and initialiser parameters, role assignments and network configuration against a written checklist before broadcasting.
Source verification.
We publish source code on the relevant block explorer (Etherscan and its multichain API, Blockscout, or Sourcify) so anyone can confirm the deployed bytecode matches the reviewed code.
Admin hand-over.
We transfer privileged roles from the deployer to your multisig or timelock and remove deployer permissions, then confirm the hand-over on-chain.

title.v: After Launch: Monitoring, Incident Response and Maintenance

c.v: A deployed contract still needs operating.
Monitoring.
Alerts on privileged function calls, unusual outflows, oracle deviations and paused states, so your team learns about a problem from an alert rather than social media.
Emergency controls.
Pause functions held by a guardian role, plus rate limits on sensitive flows where the design allows them. These let you contain an incident while it is investigated.
Incident runbooks.
Written procedures for who does what if something goes wrong: who can pause, how signers are reached, and what users are told.
Upgrades and new versions.
Storage-layout validation, fork rehearsal, timelocked execution and re-verification for every upgrade.
Bug bounties.
We recommend a public bug bounty for contracts that hold meaningful value, and we help you define scope and severity levels.

title.v: What Drives Smart Contract Development Cost and Timeline

c.v: Smart contract development cost depends on risk and novelty far more than on lines of code. The main drivers:
How novel the logic is.
A standard token built on audited libraries is a small project. A new lending mechanism is a large one.
Value at risk.
Contracts that will hold significant funds need deeper testing and an independent audit, which is a separate budget line.
Number of contracts and integrations.
Each oracle, external protocol or bridge adds integration and testing work.
Upgradeability and governance.
Proxies, timelocks and governance add design, testing and deployment steps.
Number of networks.
Each additional chain needs its own configuration, testing and verification.
Operations after launch.
Monitoring, maintenance and bug bounty rewards are ongoing costs.

As a planning guide, discovery typically takes one to two weeks, development and testing three to eight weeks, and launch one to two weeks. Simpler contracts are faster and multi-contract protocols take longer.  You receive a written estimate after discovery.

What is smart contract development?

Smart contract development is the work of designing, writing, testing and deploying programs that run on a blockchain and enforce rules automatically. Examples include transferring tokens, releasing escrowed funds or executing a governance vote. Because deployed contracts are public and often cannot be changed, the work includes architecture, security testing and deployment planning as well as coding.
How much does smart contract development cost?

Cost depends mainly on how novel the logic is, how much value the contracts will hold, the number of integrations and networks, and whether the contracts are upgradeable. A token built on audited libraries is a small project; a new DeFi protocol is a large one. An independent audit is a separate cost. We provide a written estimate after a short discovery phase, and our cost guide gives example ranges.
How long does it take to develop a smart contract?

A simple, standards-based contract can be built and tested in a few weeks. Multi-contract systems such as lending protocols or governance frameworks typically take several months once discovery, testing, audit and deployment are included. The independent audit and fixing its findings should be planned into the timeline from the start.
Which programming language is best for smart contracts?

The network decides the language more than preference does. Solidity is the standard for Ethereum and EVM-compatible chains and has the deepest tooling and auditor pool. Rust is used for Solana programs. Go is used for Hyperledger Fabric chaincode on permissioned networks. We recommend the network first, based on your users, liquidity and cost requirements, and the language follows.
Which blockchain is best for smart contract development?

There is no single best chain. Ethereum mainnet offers the most security and liquidity at higher cost. Layer 2 networks such as Arbitrum, Optimism and Base offer EVM compatibility with lower fees. Solana suits high-throughput, low-fee applications. Permissioned ledgers suit private business networks. We weigh where your users and liquidity are, transaction costs, and the integrations you need.
Can smart contracts be upgraded after deployment?

Yes, if they are designed to be. Proxy patterns such as UUPS or Transparent proxies separate a contract's address and storage from its logic, so the logic can be replaced. Upgradeability adds trust assumptions and its own risks, so we put upgrade rights behind a multisig and timelock. Some contracts are deliberately left immutable.
How do you test smart contracts?

We combine unit and integration tests with fuzz testing, invariant testing (checking that core properties hold across long random sequences of actions), tests on a fork of the live network, static analysis and internal peer review. Gas usage is tracked in the test suite so cost regressions are caught early.
Do my smart contracts need an independent audit?

For any contract holding meaningful value, yes. Our internal testing and review reduce risk and make the audit more efficient, but an independent audit adds review by a team with no stake in the code. We prepare an audit package, coordinate with the audit firm and fix the findings. No audit can guarantee a contract is free of vulnerabilities, so we also recommend monitoring and a bug bounty.
What are the most common smart contract vulnerabilities?

The OWASP Smart Contract Top 10 (2026) lists access control flaws first, followed by business logic errors, price oracle manipulation and flash-loan-facilitated attacks. Reentrancy, unchecked external calls, arithmetic errors and proxy upgrade issues also appear. Many large losses come from compromised admin keys, which is why key management is part of our design work.
What is gas optimization?

Gas optimization reduces the fees users pay to interact with a contract. The biggest savings usually come from storage design: fewer storage writes, values packed into shared slots, and off-chain data proven with Merkle roots or signatures. Smaller gains come from compiler-friendly patterns. We measure gas in the test suite and never trade away readability or safety for marginal savings.
Can you take over or fix contracts another team wrote?

Yes. We begin with a structured review of the architecture, privileged roles, upgrade mechanism and test coverage, and give you a written report. From there we can extend, refactor, upgrade or migrate the contracts using our standard testing process.
Who owns the smart contract code?
You do. The source code, tests, deployment scripts and documentation are delivered to your repository.
What happens after a smart contract is deployed?

The source code is verified on the block explorer, admin roles are moved to your multisig or timelock, and monitoring is set up for privileged actions and unusual activity. From then on the work is operational: responding to alerts, planning upgrades through a controlled process, and maintaining documentation as the system evolves.

Tell us what you are building, whether it is a token launch, a DeFi protocol, an NFT collection, a governance system or an internal business workflow. In a scoping call we will discuss what belongs on-chain, which network fits, what the main security risks are and what a realistic timeline looks like. You will leave with a clear next step whether or not you work with us.

The independent audit and fixing its findings should be planned into the timeline from the start.

faq.q: Which programming language is best for smart contracts?

c.v: The network decides the language more than preference does. Solidity is the standard for Ethereum and EVM-compatible chains and has the deepest tooling and auditor pool. Rust is used for Solana programs. Go is used for Hyperledger Fabric chaincode on permissioned networks. We recommend the network first, based on your users, liquidity and cost requirements, and the language follows.

faq.q: Which blockchain is best for smart contract development?

c.v: There is no single best chain. Ethereum mainnet offers the most security and liquidity at higher cost. Layer 2 networks such as Arbitrum, Optimism and Base offer EVM compatibility with lower fees. Solana suits high-throughput, low-fee applications. Permissioned ledgers suit private business networks. We weigh where your users and liquidity are, transaction costs, and the integrations you need.

faq.q: Can smart contracts be upgraded after deployment?

c.v: Yes, if they are designed to be. Proxy patterns such as UUPS or Transparent proxies separate a contract's address and storage from its logic, so the logic can be replaced. Upgradeability adds trust assumptions and its own risks, so we put upgrade rights behind a multisig and timelock. Some contracts are deliberately left immutable.

faq.q: How do you test smart contracts?

c.v: We combine unit and integration tests with fuzz testing, invariant testing (checking that core properties hold across long random sequences of actions), tests on a fork of the live network, static analysis and internal peer review. Gas usage is tracked in the test suite so cost regressions are caught early.

faq.q: Do my smart contracts need an independent audit?

c.v: For any contract holding meaningful value, yes. Our internal testing and review reduce risk and make the audit more efficient, but an independent audit adds review by a team with no stake in the code. We prepare an audit package, coordinate with the audit firm and fix the findings. No audit can guarantee a contract is free of vulnerabilities, so we also recommend monitoring and a bug bounty.

faq.q: What are the most common smart contract vulnerabilities?

c.v: The OWASP Smart Contract Top 10 (2026) lists access control flaws first, followed by business logic errors, price oracle manipulation and flash-loan-facilitated attacks. Reentrancy, unchecked external calls, arithmetic errors and proxy upgrade issues also appear. Many large losses come from compromised admin keys, which is why key management is part of our design work.

faq.q: What happens after a smart contract is deployed?

c.v: The source code is verified on the block explorer, admin roles are moved to your multisig or timelock, and monitoring is set up for privileged actions and unusual activity. From then on the work is operational: responding to alerts, planning upgrades through a controlled process, and maintaining documentation as the system evolves.
